definition.text: A large geographical region with a distinctive climate, vegetation and animal life.

facts.text: A biome's community forms in response to its physical environment and regional climate.
The International Biological Program of 1964–74 popularized the concept.
Boundaries between biomes must be drawn somewhat arbitrarily because one biome changes gradually into the next.
Climate change could shift biomes so much that between 54% and 22% of land will have climates matching other biomes, and 3.6% entirely new ones.
Woody plant encroachment, which turns grass savanna into shrub savanna, is an example of a biome shift.

definition.text: The various systems ecologists use to divide the world's land into biome types, mostly by temperature and rainfall.

facts.text: In 1947 Leslie Holdridge classified climates by the effects of temperature and rainfall on vegetation.
Whittaker's scheme, using precipitation and temperature, simplified Holdridge's and is easier to use but less specific.
A WWF team divided the world into biogeographic realms and ecoregions, each with a main biome, and used it to pick the Global 200 conservation priorities.
The many competing schemes show that biomes do not fit neatly into any classification.

definition.text: A way of describing the land biosphere as it now is, divided into units shaped by lasting human use such as farming, settlement and forestry.

facts.text: Across much of Earth, crops, rangelands and cities have replaced the vegetation conventional biome systems predict.
Erle Ellis and Navin Ramankutty first named and mapped anthromes in 2008.
By 2000, over half of Earth's ice-free land had been turned into rangelands, croplands, villages and dense settlements.
While 23.4% of remote woodland anthrome is protected, only 2.3% of irrigated village anthrome is.

definition.text: A chain of secondary extinctions set off when a key species in an ecosystem dies out.

facts.text: Species most at risk depend on a few foods, rely on the lost species, or must live alongside an invasive species.
The main cause is loss of top predators, which lets prey multiply, overuse their food and then crash.
Hunting sea otters for pelts let urchins strip the kelp, leaving barrens where urchins and kelp-dependent species died out locally.

definition.text: A group of populations of different species living in the same area at the same time.

facts.text: It is also called a biocoenosis, biotic community or ecological community.
Community ecology studies how coexisting species interact, and their distribution, structure and abundance.
Each species occupies a niche, and having different niches lets species coexist.
Some species, such as foundation species, keystone species and ecosystem engineers, have outsized influence, and losing them often destabilizes the community.
Community structure is often measured through networks such as food webs.

definition.text: Two opposing views of what a community is: a tightly linked unit, or a loose set of species each responding to conditions on its own.

facts.text: Frederic Clements saw the community as a kind of superorganism with sharp boundaries.
Henry Gleason argued each species changes gradually and independently along environmental gradients, so groupings are largely by chance.

definition.text: Stephen Hubbell's theory that species in a community are functionally equivalent and their numbers change through random births and deaths.

facts.text: Equivalent species undergo ecological drift: populations fluctuate randomly while the community's total number of individuals stays constant.

definition.text: A group of species that use the same resources, or use different resources in similar ways.

facts.text: Members of a guild compete because they share resources.
Guild members need not share the same niche or be closely related.
The number of guilds in an ecosystem is called its disparity.

definition.text: The ways different species affect each other, classed by whether each side gains, loses or is unaffected.

facts.text: They include competition, predation, parasitism, mutualism and commensalism.
Mutualism benefits both species, as with Rhizobium bacteria in nodules on legume roots.
In commensalism one species benefits and the other is unaffected, like an orchid growing on a tree.
In amensalism one species harms another while staying unaffected, as tadpoles do to snails by eating their algae.
Predation and parasitism benefit one species at the other's expense.
True neutralism, where neither species is noticeably affected, is rare because communities are so interconnected.
